From a galloping horse and a man in a striped suit to creatures that act live on set: 150 years of turning movement into numbers.

1878 · A galloping horse, frozen in 12 photos (Eadweard Muybridge, for Leland Stanford)
1883 · The first marker suit (Étienne-Jules Marey)
1915 · The rotoscope (Max Fleischer, with his brother Dave)
1973 · A person made of 10 to 12 lights (Gunnar Johansson)
1983 · The Graphical Marionette (Carol Ginsberg and Delle Maxwell, MIT)
2000 · A whole film made with mocap, animated in Chennai (Pentafour Software (later Pentamedia Graphics))

captions.instagram:
How does motion capture work?

A mocap camera never sees the actor, only bright dots on black. Walk a faceless performer through a ring of infrared cameras, cross the rays that pin each marker to a fraction of a millimetre, hand the motion to a four-armed creature, solve a face from helmet-camera dots, and watch an inertial suit drift away.

→ Motion capture happens on a stage ringed by infrared cameras.
→ Reflective markers shine back, so each camera sees only bright dots.
→ One camera only gives a direction; a second ray pins the marker in 3D.
→ When an arm hides a marker from too many cameras, a gap appears.
→ The computer names every dot, then fits a skeleton inside them.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/mocapclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does motion capture work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A mocap camera never sees the actor, only bright dots on black. Walk a faceless performer through a ring of infrared cameras, cross the rays that pin each marker to a fraction of a millimetre, hand the motion to a four-armed creature, solve a face from helmet-camera dots, and watch an inertial suit drift away.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/mocapclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/mocapclear

In this video:
• The capture volume. Optical mocap happens on a stage ringed by 12 to 48 infrared cameras.
• Where rays meet. One camera only gives a direction to a dot: a ray.
• Dots to a creature. Software names every dot (labelling), fits a skeleton inside them (solving), then copies the joint rotations onto a creature (retargeting).
• Faces and fingers. A head-mounted camera watches dots on the face.
• Other ways to capture. Inertial suits use about 17 motion sensors and work anywhere, but position comes from adding up acceleration twice, so it drifts unless planted feet reset it.
• On set and cleanup. In performance capture, a tracked virtual camera shows the director the creature live in its world.

Glassbox opens one box a day: an interactive model of how something works, plus the code behind it.
